title: Quiz: The Poisson Process and Renewal Counting

questions.text: In the Poisson process derivation, the orderliness postulate P(2+ events in [t, t+Δt]) = o(Δt) says:
options: Two events cannot ever occur at exactly the same instant
Two events can occur in the same instant with probability λ²Δt²
The probability of two or more simultaneous events vanishes faster than Δt as Δt → 0, making simultaneous events negligible
Events must be separated by at least Δt time units
questions.explanation: o(Δt) means the quantity goes to zero faster than Δt: o(Δt)/Δt → 0. For simultaneous events, the probability is o(Δt) — it's not exactly zero (events CAN happen close together), but in the continuous limit, the probability of two events in an infinitesimal interval is negligible compared to the probability of one event (which is λΔt).

questions.text: The exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with the memoryless property P(W > s+t | W > s) = P(W > t) for all s,t ≥ 0.
questions.explanation: The memoryless property characterises the exponential distribution uniquely among continuous distributions (and the geometric distribution among discrete distributions). The proof: P(W>s+t)/P(W>s) = P(W>t) implies the survival function F̄(t) = P(W>t) satisfies F̄(s+t) = F̄(s)F̄(t) — a functional equation whose only decreasing solution is F̄(t) = e^{-λt}.

questions.text: If N(t) is a Poisson process with rate λ, what is P(N(3) = 5)?
questions.explanation: N(t) ~ Poisson(λt). For t=3, N(3) ~ Poisson(3λ). P(N(3)=5) = e^{-3λ}(3λ)^5/5!. With generic λ this is option B only when λ=5 (giving 15). The general form is e^{-3λ}(3λ)^5/5!. The literal answer with unspecified λ would be e^{-3λ}(3λ)^5/5! — option B with λ=5. In general: always substitute λt into the Poisson PMF.

questions.text: In a Poisson process with rate λ = 3/hour, what is the expected time until the 10th patient arrives?
questions.explanation: The n-th event time T_n ~ Gamma(n, rate=λ) with E[T_n] = n/λ. For n=10, λ=3: E[T_{10}] = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 hours. Each patient arrives at average 1/λ = 1/3 hour intervals, and we need 10, so 10 × (1/3) = 10/3 hours total.

questions.text: The ODE for P_0(t) in a Poisson process is P_0'(t) = -λP_0(t) with P_0(0)=1. What is the solution P_0(t)?
questions.explanation: The ODE P_0' = -λP_0 with P_0(0)=1 has the solution P_0(t) = e^{-λt}. This is a first-order linear ODE with constant coefficient -λ. The solution is an exponential decay, consistent with P(no events by time t) = e^{-λt}.

questions.text: If the inter-arrival times of a counting process are i.i.d. Exponential(λ), then the counting process N(t) is a Poisson process with rate λ.
questions.explanation: This is the converse of what we derived. The Poisson process can be equivalently defined by: (1) the three postulates (stationarity, independence, orderliness), OR (2) i.i.d. Exp(λ) inter-arrival times. Both definitions lead to the same process. The derivation in the lesson shows (1) implies N(t)~Poisson(λt), and the i.i.d. Exp inter-arrivals recover the same distribution.
